content: 1. When new components are identified that require further toxicological and ecotoxicological testing, the information provided should be evaluated using existing data, bridging information from similar botanicals, expert judgment, or a case-by-case approach. 2. In the Tier II decision-making process, the options include determining whether the new source poses no greater hazard and is equivalent to the reference source, or if it is not equivalent due to presenting a greater hazard. 3. Botanicals are not inherently non-toxic, and risk mitigation measures may be necessary to minimize risks to human health. Where sufficient documented knowledge exists, it should be used to avoid unnecessary animal testing. 4. Evaluators may accept extrapolation (read-across) from one botanical active substance to another concerning the same toxicological components of concern, provided there is evidence of their composition regarding the specific components of concern. 5. Reference values and high-quality assessments from other regulatory frameworks may be considered if the basis for deriving these thresholds can be evaluated. For example, epidemiological studies may be used, but applicants are advised to discuss this approach early with the pesticide board. 6. If there is no indication of concern, a scientific justification may suffice to confirm no unacceptable risks. However, if concerns are reasonably expected, results from suitable studies (acute and longer-term if adverse findings arise from acute studies) should be presented and assessed. 7. When components of concern with known toxic properties are present in the technical grade under evaluation, the significance of overall exposure should be assessed and compared with existing health-based guidance values, such as the acceptable/tolerable daily intake (ADI/TDI). 8. Consideration of exposure to components of concern in relation to Threshold of Toxicological Concern (TTC) values may also be helpful. Guidance on the applicability of the TTC concept can be found in the EFSA journal. 9. If components of concern are identified and additional toxicological data are deemed necessary, hazard identification should focus on these specific components. If no components of concern are identified, complete identification and characterization are generally required. 10. It is acknowledged that identifying the active principle responsible for an adverse effect may be challenging. However, the submitted information must be sufficient to assess whether the botanical active substance meets the relevant approval criteria. 11. Secondary plant compounds in botanicals are common in nature, and human and environmental exposure to many of them is frequent. Quantifying this exposure may be complex, but well-documented exposure assessments exist for some substances. 12. If the proposed botanical is considered the same material reasonably expected to be or become a food component, this provides significant reassurance for consumer exposure. However, applicants must provide evidence that the material complies with relevant food legislation and explain its use in food. 13. For many botanical active substances, residue data may not be required if detectable residues on consumable commodities are unlikely to occur, or if residue levels are unlikely to exceed natural exposure and are not of toxicological concern. 14. When natural or documented exposures are considered to address consumer exposure, a detailed consumer risk assessment comparing anticipated exposures from intended use to background exposures should be presented. 15. If technically feasible, synthesizing and radiolabeling the active components or known toxicological components may be required, and standard data requirements on metabolism would apply. 16. When residues on food or feed cannot be excluded, a consumer exposure assessment will be required. 17. Arguments related to natural exposure must be carefully considered. Estimated exposures of botanical components should be compared to natural exposure situations in relevant environmental compartments (water, soil, air). 18. The risk is acceptable when estimated exposures are lower than or similar to natural exposure situations and no unacceptable effects occur. If estimated exposures exceed natural levels, more information may be needed to assess relevant exposure levels, addressing persistence, transformation, and mobility in the environment. 19. Botanicals are complex mixtures with multiple components, and the entire technical grade is regarded as the active substance. However, studies with single active components may provide more reliable information on fate and behavior properties, though they may behave differently than the whole botanical active substance. 20. If technically feasible, synthesizing and radiolabeling active components or known environmental concern components may be required, and standard data requirements would apply. 21. Components from botanicals are found in plants, and common pathways for their breakdown and decomposition in plants and the environment are expected. Therefore, data on environmental fate could be waived in some cases. 22. Ecotoxicological risks are acceptable when estimated exposures are lower than or similar to natural exposure situations and no unacceptable effects occur on relevant non-target organisms. The activity, mode of action, and exposure route of the botanical should be considered to focus on non-target organisms most at risk and avoid unnecessary animal testing. 23. Due to the diversity and complexity of botanicals, non-target organisms potentially affected vary substantially, and a general testing strategy cannot be provided. Applicants should develop a relevant testing strategy based on proposed uses and exposure situations. 24. Available ecotoxicological information, including studies and publications, should be analyzed and considered. High-quality assessments from other regulatory frameworks may also be taken into account. 25. If estimated exposures exceed natural levels, more information is needed to assess the possible effect on exposed non-target organisms. Identifying the active principle responsible for an unacceptable effect may be challenging, but the submitted information must be sufficient to assess whether the botanical meets the relevant approval criteria. 26. Efficacy data are necessary to protect users from unrealistic claims by manufacturers and to ensure the quality of botanical products. Botanical products must demonstrate sufficient effectiveness to justify their label claims. 27. Botanical products may have multiple modes of action, making it challenging to assess their effects in trials. Efficacy testing should demonstrate that the botanical product provides sufficient benefits to outweigh any negative effects. 28. As a minimum, there should be a statistically significant improvement in an appropriate measure of pest control or crop yield, of sufficient magnitude to be worthwhile from a user's perspective. 29. Data from good quality and representative field trials are generally required. Data from small-scale laboratory or growth chamber studies may complement the overall data package, reducing the number of field/glasshouse trials needed. 30. For plant protection uses, relevant EPPO guidelines can be referred to for guidance. However, deviations from the guidance may be required to account for the specific properties of botanical products, with detailed descriptions and explanations provided. 31. For public health, applicants should follow guidance on suitable testing methods where available. All trials should include an untreated control, and an appropriately justified reference product should also be included in most trials. 32. Variation in the efficacy of botanical products for pest control may be greater than expected for conventional chemical pesticides. Botanical products may provide full control, partial control, or contribute to control. 33. Reduced performance should not automatically lead to refusal of authorization if the applicant provides reasons why the demonstrated efficacy might be sufficient, such as offering an alternative mode of action, valuable uses, resistance management, or compatibility with IPM or IVM systems. 34. As a minimum, there must always be a statistically significant improvement, at an acceptable level of probability, of an appropriate measure, of sufficient magnitude to be worthwhile from a user's perspective. 35. It should be possible to extrapolate trial data from areas with comparable climates, limiting the number of additional trials required. For some areas, such as non-target plant effects, information may be used in lieu of actual data. 36. Applicants and evaluating officials should focus on ensuring that users are provided with accurate information on the likely performance of the botanical product and advice on how best to use it for effective and consistent results. 37. Definitions are harmonized with other international sources such as OECD, US EPA, and EU to ensure consistency.
